meta.title: Who really said "Prostitution in towns is like the sewer in a palace; take away the sewers and the palace becomes an impure and stinking place"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Aquinas: the palace-sewer line paraphrases Ptolemy of Lucca's continuation of De regimine principum (c. 1300), which credits the image to Augustine.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Prostitution in towns is like the sewer in a palace; take away the sewers and the palace becomes an impure and stinking place'?
meta.ogDescription: Often pinned on Thomas Aquinas, the palace-sewer line comes from Ptolemy of Lucca's continuation of De regimine principum, Book 4, not from Aquinas.

answer.label: Not Thomas Aquinas — actually Ptolemy of Lucca
answer.authorDates: c. 1236 – c. 1327 · Dominican friar, historian & bishop of Torcello
answer.sourceLine: The popular line paraphrases a passage in Book 4, chapter 14 of De regimine principum (On the Government of Rulers). Aquinas began that treatise, but Ptolemy of Lucca wrote Book 4 when he completed it around 1300. Ptolemy credits the sewer image to Augustine, yet the genuine Augustine passage (De ordine 2.4.12) mentions no sewer. See Wikiquote ↗.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: De regimine principum (continuation of Aquinas’s De regno), Book 4, ch. 14
James M. Blythe, On the Government of Rulers (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997), 4.14.6

source.excerpt: Unde Augustinus dicit, quod hoc facit meretrix in mundo, quod sentina in mari, vel cloaca in palatio: tolle cloacam, et replebis foetore palatium: et similiter de sentina: tolle meretrices de mundo, et replebis ipsum sodomia.
trail: Wikiquote’s Thomas Aquinas page ↗ lists the line as Misattributed. It identifies the source as Ptolemy of Lucca’s continuation of De regimine principum (Blythe translation, 1997, 4.14.6), and notes that only Book 1 and the first four chapters of Book 2 are by Aquinas.
The Latin passage appears under Liber 4, Caput 14 in Corpus Thomisticum’s text of Ptolemy’s Continuatio S. Thomae De regno ↗. That text is separate from Aquinas’s own De regno ad regem Cypri ↗.
The catalog record for Blythe’s translation ↗ (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997) says Ptolemy finished the work around 1300, completing a treatise long attributed to Aquinas.
Wikipedia ↗ says Ptolemy completed De Regimine Principum after Aquinas died and wrote Books 3 and 4.
source.excerptNote: Blythe’s English, as quoted on Wikiquote ↗, reads: “Thus, Augustine says that a whore acts in the world as the bilge in a ship or the sewer in a palace: ‘Remove the sewer, and you will fill the palace with a stench.’” The phrases “in towns” and “impure and stinking place” appear in neither the Latin nor that translation.

source.rightsNote: The popular English wording is an anonymous paraphrase with no identifiable source, so we assert no rights status for it. The Latin original (completed around 1300) is long in the public domain. Blythe’s 1997 English translation (University of Pennsylvania Press) is a modern rendering still in copyright.

author.name: Ptolemy of Lucca
author.heading: About Ptolemy of Lucca
author.metaLine: c. 1236 – c. 1327 · Dominican friar, historian & bishop of Torcello
author.bio: Ptolemy (Tolomeo) of Lucca was a Dominican friar who was a friend and confessor of Thomas Aquinas. In 1318 Pope John XXII made him bishop of Torcello. After Aquinas died, Ptolemy completed Aquinas’s unfinished treatise on kingship, De regimine principum, and wrote Books 3 and 4 himself. Because the finished work long circulated under Aquinas’s name, Ptolemy’s words, including this passage, have often been credited to Aquinas.

misattribution.heading: How Aquinas got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is pinned on Thomas Aquinas because the treatise it comes from began as his. Aquinas left De regimine principum unfinished, Ptolemy of Lucca completed it, and the whole work long circulated under Aquinas’s name.

items.why: Aquinas did not write the part of the treatise that holds the passage. Wikiquote ↗ notes that the work mentions the 1298 coronation of Albert I of Habsburg. Aquinas died in 1274 ↗.
Ptolemy wrote Book 4, chapter 14, where the bilge-and-sewer comparison appears in the Latin text ↗.

Ptolemy introduces the image with “Augustinus dicit”. But Wikiquote ↗ gives what Augustine actually wrote in De ordine 2.4.12: “Remove prostitutes from human affairs and you will unsettle everything on account of lusts.” That passage has no sewer and no palace.

misattribution.truthLine: The image of the sewer in the palace is Ptolemy of Lucca’s elaboration of a milder line from Augustine. The tidy English version credited to Aquinas is a later paraphrase of Ptolemy (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: What the passage was arguing
lead: In the Latin text ↗, the sentence comes in a discussion of soldiers and marriage. Ptolemy reports that Aristotle rejects Plato’s view that men devoted to war should not marry. He then gives his reasoning: relations with women are a lesser evil than falling into “vile vices”. The sewer comparison is offered in support of that point.
So the passage is a medieval “necessary evil” argument for tolerating prostitution, put in Augustine’s mouth. It is neither a statement by Aquinas nor Augustine’s own words.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the line as Misattributed to Aquinas and gives the source as Ptolemy of Lucca's continuation (Blythe trans., 1997, 4.14.6). It quotes Blythe's bilge/sewer wording, gives Augustine De ordine 2.4.12 as 'Remove prostitutes from human affairs and you will unsettle everything on account of lusts', says only Book 1 and the first four chapters of Book 2 are by Aquinas, and notes the mention of Albert I's 1298 coronation.

The Latin text of Ptolemy's Continuatio S. Thomae De regno, Liber 4 Caput 14, contains 'hoc facit meretrix in mundo, quod sentina in mari, vel cloaca in palatio: tolle cloacam, et replebis foetore palatium'. The passage sits in a discussion of Aristotle rejecting Plato on soldiers marrying.
Corpus Thomisticum hosts Aquinas's own De regno ad regem Cypri as a separate text.

Blythe's translation On the Government of Rulers (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997) carries the subtitle 'Ptolemy of Lucca with Portions Attributed to Thomas Aquinas'. Its description says Ptolemy finished the work around 1300.
Ptolemy of Lucca (c. 1236 – c. 1327) was a Dominican, a friend and confessor of Aquinas, and from 1318 bishop of Torcello. He completed De Regimine Principum, writing Books 3 and 4.
